summary.big_en: Every substance has its own melting temperature and its own boiling temperature.

rows.a: Only at its own boiling point

points.t: Ice melts at 0 °C, but gold melts at 1064 °C.
Pure water boils at 100 °C, but vinegar boils at 118 °C.
Two matching balloons on a ruler balance show that gas has mass.

watch_out.wrong: Evaporation only happens when you heat a liquid.
watch_out.right: Evaporation can happen at any temperature, even in the cold.

watch_out.wrong: Air is empty space and does not weigh anything.
watch_out.right: Air is made of gases, which take up space and have mass.

watch_out.wrong: Heat a bigger pan of water and its boiling point goes up.
watch_out.right: Water always boils at 100 °C, no matter how much of it you heat.

from_the_book.activity: Blow up two balloons to the same size, tie them to a ruler balance, then let the air out of one.
from_the_book.what_it_shows: The balloon still full of air pulls its side down — gases have mass.

glossary.def: A special feature of a substance that helps us tell it apart from other things.
glossary.example: Gold melts at 1064 °C — that helps us identify it.

glossary.def: Anything that takes up space and has mass.
glossary.example: Air is a mixture of gases that takes up space.

glossary.def: The amount of material that makes up an object.
glossary.example: The air inside a blown-up balloon has mass we can measure.

glossary.def: The exact temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
glossary.example: Ice changes into liquid water at 0 °C.

glossary.def: A liquid loses heat and turns into a solid.
glossary.example: Liquid water turns into ice when cooled to 0 °C.

glossary.def: The exact temperature where all of a liquid gets enough energy to turn into a gas.
glossary.example: Pure water changes into a gas at 100 °C.

glossary.def: A fast change where particles all through the liquid turn into a gas when heated.
glossary.example: Water bubbling on a hot plate at 100 °C.

glossary.def: A slow change where only the particles on the surface of a liquid turn into a gas.
glossary.example: Water slowly disappearing from a shallow dish at room temperature.

glossary.def: A gas cools down and turns back into a liquid.
glossary.example: Water droplets forming on a cool surface when steam cools.

summary.big_en: Metals are super helpers: they let heat and electricity flow straight through.

points.t: Silver is the best heat conductor — but pots aren't made of it because silver costs too much.
Some pots have a copper bottom: copper heats up quickly.
Copper wires carry electricity, and even a steel paper clip can light a lamp.
Graphite in a pencil conducts too — a 2 cm piece lights the lamp brighter than a 10 cm piece.
Hot tea stays warm longest in a polystyrene foam cup.

watch_out.wrong: A metal dish feels warmer than a plastic dish when both hold an ice cube.
watch_out.right: The plastic feels warmer. Metal pulls heat away from your fingers faster, so it feels colder.
Graphite inside a pencil is a non-metal and still lights a lamp.

watch_out.wrong: A wooden spoon gets hot and burns your hand when you stir soup.
watch_out.right: Wood conducts heat poorly, so it stays cool and is safe to hold.

from_the_book.activity: Metal spoon, plastic spoon, glass rod, pencil and polystyrene foam put into hot water, each with a bead stuck on using petroleum jelly.
from_the_book.what_it_shows: The bead on the metal spoon falls off first — metal carries heat fastest and melts the jelly.

glossary.def: The way heat moves from a hot object to a colder one when they touch.
glossary.example: A metal teaspoon in hot tea gets warm.

glossary.def: A material that lets heat travel through it quickly and easily.
glossary.example: Copper on the bottom of a pan.

glossary.def: A material that does not let heat pass through it easily.
glossary.example: A polystyrene foam cup keeps tea warm.

glossary.def: A material that lets electricity flow through it easily.
glossary.example: A steel paper clip can light a lamp in a circuit.

glossary.def: A material that stops electricity flowing through it.
glossary.example: The plastic handle of a pan.

glossary.def: A complete loop that electricity flows around.
glossary.example: A lamp, a cell and copper connecting wires joined in a loop.

summary.big_en: You can undo a reversible change and get your starting materials back. An irreversible change is forever.

rows.a: Yes — it goes back to how it was
rows.b: No — never back to the start

rows.a: No, only looks or feels different

rows.b: Burning a match; rust on a tin can

points.t: Ice cubes on a saucer in the sun melt in about five minutes.
Burning a wooden match turns it into a black substance called carbon.
Jelly powder + boiling water makes a liquid that sets solid in the fridge.
Sugar dissolves in 90 seconds at 20 °C, but only 15 seconds at 80 °C.
Melting butter in a pan can be reversed. Baking a cake cannot.

watch_out.wrong: Dissolved sugar is gone forever because you can't see it.
watch_out.right: It is still there — its tiny particles have spread out evenly through the water.

watch_out.wrong: Boiling an egg is reversible because you only heat it.
watch_out.right: It is irreversible: a cooked egg can never go back to raw.

watch_out.wrong: You must stir sugar or it won't dissolve.
watch_out.right: Sugar dissolves by itself if you leave it in water long enough — stirring just makes it faster.

from_the_book.activity: Put ice cubes on a saucer in the sun, then place the melted water back in the freezer.
from_the_book.what_it_shows: Melting and freezing are reversible physical changes — the water changes back and forth.

glossary.def: A change in how a substance looks or feels, without turning it into a new substance.
glossary.example: Solid ice melting to become liquid water.

glossary.def: A change that can be undone so the material goes back to the way it was.
glossary.example: Freezing liquid water back into ice.

glossary.def: A change that cannot be undone to get the original material back.
glossary.example: Burning a wooden match so it turns into black carbon.

glossary.def: To mix a solid completely into a liquid so its parts spread out evenly and you can no longer see them.
glossary.example: Salt mixing into water to make salty sea water.

glossary.def: The solid that is mixed into a liquid and seems to disappear.
glossary.example: Sugar added to a cup of warm tea.

glossary.def: The liquid that a solid is mixed into.
glossary.example: The water in a jar used to mix with sugar.

glossary.def: A mixture of a solid and a liquid that is spread out evenly and looks the same throughout.
glossary.example: Water and sugar after stirring.

glossary.def: Looking exactly the same in every part of a mixture.
glossary.example: Salt water where you cannot see any salt pieces.

glossary.def: How fast or slow something happens.
glossary.example: How quickly sugar mixes into hot water compared to cold.

summary.big_en: Mix substances together and sometimes you get a brand new substance — one you cannot easily change back.

points.t: Vinegar + bicarbonate of soda bubbles up and makes carbon dioxide gas.
Pour vinegar on wire wool in a beaker: after five minutes the thermometer shows the temperature has risen.
Magnesium burns in oxygen with a bright white flame and leaves a white powder.
Heat iron and sulfur together and you get a new substance: iron sulfide.
An iron nail left in a saucer of water for a few days grows orange-brown rust.

watch_out.wrong: A candle melting is a chemical reaction.
watch_out.right: Melting wax is only a change of state. The burning wick is the chemical reaction.

watch_out.wrong: Dissolving sugar is a chemical reaction because the sugar disappears.
watch_out.right: Dissolving is a physical change — evaporate the water and the sugar comes back.

watch_out.wrong: Any bubbles in water mean a chemical reaction.
watch_out.right: Bubbles in boiling water are just water turning to gas. Bubbles from vinegar + baking soda are a real reaction.

from_the_book.activity: Loosen some wire wool, put it in a beaker, pour vinegar on it and measure the temperature with a thermometer.
from_the_book.what_it_shows: After five minutes the temperature rises — a chemical reaction can give out heat.

glossary.def: Different materials mix and change into completely new materials that cannot easily be turned back.
glossary.example: Vinegar and bicarbonate of soda making a new gas.

glossary.def: When materials mix and change each other to make a new material.
glossary.example: Bicarbonate of soda and vinegar changing each other when they touch.

glossary.def: One of the materials you start with, before a chemical change happens.
glossary.example: Bicarbonate of soda in the jar experiment.

glossary.def: A new material that is made after a chemical change.
glossary.example: The carbon dioxide bubbles made in the vinegar experiment.

glossary.def: Signs we can see, hear or feel that prove a change has happened.
glossary.example: The bubbles when vinegar and bicarbonate of soda are mixed.

glossary.def: A permanent change that cannot be undone to get the original materials back.
glossary.example: A burnt candle wick turning to black carbon.

glossary.def: A rough, orange-brown material that forms on iron left in wet conditions.
glossary.example: The orange-brown layer on an iron nail left in water.

quiz.stem_en: What is the melting point of ice?
quiz.why_en: Ice melts and becomes liquid water at a temperature of 0 °C.

quiz.stem_en: Why is the melting point of a substance always lower than its boiling point?

choices.en: Particles need less energy to slide past each other than to completely break apart as a gas.
Substances always boil before they melt.
Cooling makes particles move much faster.
Melting only happens at very high temperatures.

quiz.why_en: It takes less energy to melt a solid into a liquid than to boil a liquid into a gas.

quiz.stem_en: What is the boiling point of pure water?
quiz.why_en: Pure water boils at a temperature of 100 °C.

quiz.stem_en: What is the main difference between boiling and evaporation?

choices.en: Boiling happens only on the surface of the liquid.
Evaporation happens throughout the whole liquid.
Boiling happens throughout the liquid, while evaporation only happens on the surface.
Evaporation only happens when we heat a liquid to a very high temperature.

quiz.why_en: Boiling happens throughout the liquid, but evaporation only happens at the surface.

quiz.stem_en: If we heat 100 ml of water, vinegar, and olive oil on the same burner, which liquid will turn into a gas first?

choices.en: Olive oil because it has the highest boiling point of 300 °C.
Water because it has the lowest boiling point of 100 °C.
Vinegar because it boils at 118 °C.
They will all turn into gas at the exact same time.

quiz.why_en: The liquid with the lowest boiling point will turn into a gas first.

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is a property of all gases?

choices.en: They have no mass and take up no space.
They have mass and take up space.
They only exist when we heat them.
They have a fixed shape like solids.

quiz.why_en: All matter, including gases, has mass and takes up space.

quiz.stem_en: What do we call materials that conduct heat very well?

choices.en: Thermal insulators
Thermal conductors
Electrical conductors
Electrical insulators

quiz.why_en: Substances and materials that conduct heat well are called thermal conductors.

quiz.stem_en: Why are the handles of cooking pots and pans usually made of plastic?

choices.en: Plastic is a metal that cools down very quickly.
Plastic is not a good conductor of heat, so it stops your hand from getting burnt.
Plastic is the best conductor of heat.
Plastic helps transfer heat from the stove to the food.

quiz.why_en: Plastic is a poor thermal conductor, so heat does not travel through it easily to burn your hand.

quiz.stem_en: Which of these materials is the best conductor of heat?

choices.en: Stainless steel
Copper
Silver
Aluminium

quiz.why_en: The Learner's Book states that silver is the best conductor of heat.

quiz.stem_en: What metal is the connecting wire inside electrical circuits usually made of?

choices.en: Plastic
Copper
Glass
Wood

quiz.why_en: Connecting wires are made of copper because copper conducts electricity.

quiz.stem_en: Which non-metal (phi kim) substance is able to conduct electricity in a circuit?

choices.en: Pencil graphite
Sugar
Polystyrene foam
Glass rod

quiz.why_en: Graphite is a form of carbon that can conduct electricity in a circuit.

quiz.stem_en: Why are electrical plugs and covers made of plastic?

choices.en: Plastic conducts electricity better than copper.
Plastic is an electrical insulator, which stops electricity from flowing into your body.
Plastic makes the electric current flow much faster.
Plastic is a metal that is very cheap.

quiz.why_en: Plastic is an electrical insulator and does not conduct electricity.

quiz.stem_en: What is a physical change?

choices.en: A change that makes a completely new substance.
A change that only alters how a substance looks or feels, without making a new substance.
A change that can never be reversed.
A change caused only by burning things.

quiz.why_en: A physical change does not change a substance into a different substance.

quiz.stem_en: Which of these processes is an irreversible change?

choices.en: Melting butter in a hot pan
Freezing water into ice
Baking a cake
Dissolving salt in water

quiz.why_en: Baking a cake causes chemical changes that cannot be reversed to get the original ingredients back.

quiz.stem_en: In a salt water solution, what are the scientific names for the salt and the water?

choices.en: Salt is the solvent, and water is the solute.
Salt is the solute, and water is the solvent.
Both salt and water are solutes.
Salt is the reactant, and water is the product.

quiz.why_en: The solid in a solution is the solute, and the liquid is the solvent.

quiz.stem_en: Why is dissolving salt in water called a reversible change?

choices.en: Because the salt disappears forever.
Because we can evaporate the water to leave the solid salt behind.
Because we can freeze the solution to separate them.
Because salt changes into water particles.

quiz.why_en: Evaporating the liquid solvent leaves the solid solute behind, which reverses the dissolving.

quiz.stem_en: How does water temperature affect how fast sugar dissolves?

choices.en: Sugar dissolves faster in cold water than in hot water.
Sugar dissolves faster in hot water than in cold water.
Temperature does not affect how fast sugar dissolves.
Hot water stops sugar from dissolving at all.

quiz.why_en: Sugar and other solids dissolve faster in hot water than in cold water.

quiz.stem_en: Using the particle model, why does sugar dissolve faster in hot water?

choices.en: Hot water makes the sugar particles grow much bigger.
In hot water, particles have more energy and move faster, which helps them spread out quickly.
Cold water makes the water particles disappear.
Hot water makes the sugar particles stay completely still.

quiz.why_en: Higher temperature increases particle energy and movement, making dissolving faster.

quiz.stem_en: When an iron nail is left in water and rusts, what are the reactants and the product?

choices.en: The reactants are iron, water, and oxygen; the product is rust.
The reactant is rust; the products are iron and water.
The reactants are rust and water; the product is iron.
There are no reactants because rusting is a physical change.

quiz.why_en: Iron reacts with water and oxygen from the air to form the new product, rust.

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is NOT reliable evidence that a chemical reaction has taken place?

choices.en: Bubbles of gas form when we mix vinegar and baking soda.
A solid candle wax melts and turns into a liquid when heated.
A bright white flame is seen when burning magnesium.
An egg rots and forms a gas that smells very bad.

quiz.why_en: Melting candle wax is a physical change of state, not a chemical reaction, because no new substance is formed.

quiz.stem_en: Which metal is the best conductor of heat?

choices.en: Copper
Silver
Aluminium
Iron

quiz.why_en: According to the Learner's Book, silver is the best conductor of heat, even though other metals like copper also conduct heat well.

quiz.stem_en: What is a thermal conductor?

choices.en: A material that lets electricity pass through it easily.
A material that does not let heat pass through it.
A material that lets heat pass through it easily.
A material that does not let electricity pass through it.

quiz.why_en: A thermal conductor is a material or substance that conducts heat well (lets heat pass through easily). Electrical conductors let electricity pass through easily.

quiz.stem_en: A metal teaspoon handle becomes warm when you put it in a hot cup of tea. Which property of the metal spoon does this show?

choices.en: It is a good thermal conductor.
It is a good electrical conductor.
It is a good electrical insulator.
It has a low boiling point.

quiz.why_en: When heat from the hot tea moves to the teaspoon handle, it shows conduction of heat. This means the metal is a good thermal conductor. It does not involve electricity.

quiz.stem_en: Electric wires are often made of copper. Why do we use copper for electric wires?

choices.en: Because copper is the best conductor of heat.
Because copper is a good electrical insulator.
Because copper is a non-metal.
Because copper conducts electricity well.

quiz.why_en: We use copper in electric wires because it conducts electricity well (it is an electrical conductor). Silver is the best conductor of heat, but copper wires are used for circuits.
